One-dimensional optimization

Newton, gradient descent, and quasi-Newton methods

Multi-dimensional optimization with `optim()`: maximum likelihood

Constrained problems and linear programming

::: notes - Rizzo Chapter 14 (Sections 14.1-14.3 and 14.5). The EM algorithm (14.4) has its own deck. ::: ## Optimization Is Everywhere in Statistics - Maximum likelihood: $\hat\theta = \argmax_\theta\ell(\theta)$ - Least squares, ridge, lasso: $\argmin_\beta\ \text{RSS} + \lambda\,\text{penalty}$ - K-means: $\argmin_{C, c}\sum_k\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - c_k\|^2$ - Neural networks: minimize a loss over millions of weights - Bandwidth selection: minimize UCV$(h)$ R's toolbox: `optimize()` (1-d), `optim()` (Nelder-Mead, BFGS, CG, L-BFGS-B, SANN, Brent), `nlm()`, `nlminb()`, `constrOptim()`, `boot::simplex()` (linear programming). ## Example 14.1: One-Dimensional Optimization Maximize $f(x) = \dfrac{\log(x + \log x)}{\log(1+x)}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(x) log(x + log(x)) / log(1 + x) curve(f(x), from = 2, to = 15, ylab = "f(x)", lwd = 3, col = "#003366") opt <- optimize(f, lower = 4, upper = 8, maximum = TRUE) abline(v = opt$maximum, lty = 2, col = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/18-optimization/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} unlist(opt) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` maximum objective 5.792 1.055 ``` ::: ::: - `optimize` uses golden-section search with parabolic interpolation; it finds a **local** optimum in the interval. ## Golden-Section Search by Hand Keep a bracket $[a,b]$ and two interior points at the golden ratio $\phi = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2$; each step discards a fraction $1-\phi\approx 0.382$ of the bracket using **one** new function evaluation. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} golden <- function(f, a, b, tol = 1e-8) { phi <- (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2; x1 <- b - phi * (b - a); x2 <- a + phi * (b - a); f1 <- f(x1); f2 <- f(x2); k <- 0 while (b - a > tol) { k <- k + 1 if (f1 > f2) { b <- x2; x2 <- x1; f2 <- f1; x1 <- b - phi * (b - a); f1 <- f(x1) } # maximize else { a <- x1; x1 <- x2; f1 <- f2; x2 <- a + phi * (b - a); f2 <- f(x2) } } c(maximum = (a + b) / 2, iterations = k) } golden(f, 4, 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` maximum iterations 5.792 42.000 ``` ::: ::: ## Newton's Method and Its Relatives To maximize $\ell(\theta)$, solve $\nabla\ell(\theta) = \mathbf 0$ with Newton's method: $$ \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \big[\nabla^2\ell(\theta_k)\big]^{-1}\nabla\ell(\theta_k). $$ | Method | Uses | Convergence | Cost per step | |---|---|---|---| | Gradient ascent | $\nabla\ell$ | linear | cheap | | Newton-Raphson | $\nabla\ell$, $\nabla^2\ell$ | quadratic (near optimum) | Hessian + solve | | Fisher scoring | $\nabla\ell$, $\mathcal I(\theta)$ | ~quadratic | expected information | | Quasi-Newton (BFGS) | $\nabla\ell$, Hessian approximation | superlinear | cheap updates | | Nelder-Mead | $\ell$ only | slow, robust | function evaluations | ## Gradient Descent vs. Newton on a Quadratic ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} A <- matrix(c(3, 1.4, 1.4, 1), 2); b <- c(1, 1) fq <- function(x) 0.5 * sum(x * (A %*% x)) - sum(b * x) # minimum at solve(A, b) gq <- function(x) as.vector(A %*% x - b) gd <- function(x, step = 0.25, n = 40) { path <- x; for (k in 1:n) { x <- x - step * gq(x); path <- rbind(path, x) }; path } nt <- function(x, n = 2) { path <- x; for (k in 1:n) { x <- x - solve(A, gq(x)); path <- rbind(path, x) }; path } g1 <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100); z <- outer(g1, g1, Vectorize(function(u, v) fq(c(u, v)))) contour(g1, g1, z, nlevels = 25, col = "gray60", asp = 1, xlab = expression(theta[1]), ylab = expression(theta[2])) lines(gd(c(-2.5, 2.5)), type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#C0392B", lwd = 2) lines(nt(c(-2.5, 2.5)), type = "b", pch = 17, col = "#003366", lwd = 3, cex = 1.5) legend("topright", c("gradient descent (40 steps)", "Newton (1 step!)"), col = c("#C0392B", "#003366"), lwd = 2, pch = c(19, 17), bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/18-optimization/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 14.2: MLE for the Gamma Distribution $$ \ell(r,\lambda) = nr\log\lambda + (r-1)\sum\log x_i - \lambda\sum x_i - n\log\Gamma(r). $$ Setting $\partial\ell/\partial\lambda = 0$ gives $\lambda = r/\bar x$; substituting, $r$ solves the **one**-dimensional equation $$ \log r - \psi(r) = \log\bar x - \overline{\log x}\qquad(\psi = \text{digamma}). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); m <- 2000; est <- matrix(0, m, 2); n <- 200; r <- 5; lambda <- 2 obj <- function(r, x) log(r) - digamma(r) - (log(mean(x)) - mean(log(x))) for (i in 1:m) { x <- rgamma(n, shape = r, rate = lambda) u <- uniroot(obj, lower = .001, upper = 10e5, x = x) est[i, ] <- c(u$root, u$root / mean(x)) } colMeans(est) # close to (5, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.064 2.028 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 14.3: Two-Dimensional Optimization with `optim` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} LL <- function(theta, sx, slogx, n) { r <- theta[1]; lambda <- theta[2] loglik <- n * r * log(lambda) + (r - 1) * slogx - lambda * sx - n * log(gamma(r)) -loglik } set.seed(4750); n <- 200; x <- rgamma(n, shape = 5, rate = 2) optim(c(1, 1), LL, sx = sum(x), slogx = sum(log(x)), n = n)[c("par", "value", "counts", "convergence")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $par [1] 4.670 1.879 $value [1] 296.6 $counts function gradient 73 NA $convergence [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: - Default method is **Nelder-Mead** (no derivatives). Try `method = "BFGS"` with an analytic gradient: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} grLL <- function(theta, sx, slogx, n) { r <- theta[1]; lambda <- theta[2] -c(n * log(lambda) + slogx - n * digamma(r), n * r / lambda - sx) } fit <- optim(c(1, 1), LL, grLL, sx = sum(x), slogx = sum(log(x)), n = n, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(1e-4, 1e-4), hessian = TRUE) rbind(estimate = fit$par, se = sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] estimate 4.6701 1.8795 se 0.4513 0.1918 ``` ::: ::: ## Reparametrize Instead of Constraining $r, \lambda > 0$: optimize over $(\log r, \log\lambda)\in\R^2$; use `lgamma()` not `log(gamma())` (Ch 13!). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} LL2 <- function(eta, x) -sum(dgamma(x, shape = exp(eta[1]), rate = exp(eta[2]), log = TRUE)) fit2 <- optim(c(0, 0), LL2, x = x, method = "BFGS") exp(fit2$par) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.670 1.879 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip Good practice for `optim`: sensible starting values (MOM!), unconstrained parametrization, analytic gradients when available, check `convergence == 0`, and try more than one start. ::: ## Example 14.4: MLE for a Quadratic Form (a Mixture) $Y = \lambda_1X_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_kX_k^2$ in distribution is an equal mixture of Gamma$\big(\tfrac12, \tfrac1{2\lambda_j}\big)$ (here $k = 3$, $\sum\lambda_j = 1$). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} LL <- function(lambda, y) { lambda3 <- 1 - sum(lambda) f1 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda[1])) f2 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda[2])) f3 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda3)) f <- f1 / 3 + f2 / 3 + f3 / 3 # density of mixture return(-sum(log(f))) # returning -loglikelihood } set.seed(9); m <- 2000 lambda <- c(.6, .25, .15) # rate is 1/(2lambda) lam <- sample(lambda, size = 2000, replace = TRUE) y <- rgamma(m, shape = .5, rate = 1 / (2 * lam)) opt <- optim(c(.5, .3), LL, y = y) c(opt$par, 1 - sum(opt$par)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5890 0.2505 0.1605 ``` ::: ::: - Next lecture: the **EM algorithm** solves the same problem (Example 14.5) without derivatives. ## Simulated Annealing (`method = "SANN"`) For rough or multimodal objectives, accept "uphill" moves with probability $e^{-\Delta/T}$ and lower the temperature $T$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rough <- function(x) (x[1]^2 + x[2]^2) / 20 - cos(3 * x[1]) * cos(3 * x[2]) # many local minima set.seed(4750) starts <- matrix(runif(20, -4, 4), 10) bfgs <- apply(starts, 1, function(s) optim(s, rough, method = "BFGS")$value) sann <- apply(starts, 1, function(s) optim(s, rough, method = "SANN", control = list(maxit = 5000))$value) boxplot(list(BFGS = bfgs, SANN = sann), horizontal = TRUE, col = c("#88A0C8", "#FFCC00"), main = "Final objective from 10 random starts (global min = -1)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/18-optimization/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: # Linear Programming ## Example 14.6: The Simplex Algorithm Maximize $2x + 2y + 3z$ subject to $-2x + y + z\le 1$, $\ 4x - y + 3z\le 3$, $\ x, y, z\ge 0$. - If an optimum exists, it is attained at a **vertex** of the feasible polytope; the simplex method moves from vertex to vertex in the direction of greatest increase. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(boot) A1 <- rbind(c(-2, 1, 1), c(4, -1, 3)); b1 <- c(1, 3); a <- c(2, 2, 3) s <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, maxi = TRUE) s$soln; s$value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x1 x2 x3 2 5 0 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` b 14 ``` ::: ::: ::: question The solution is $(x, y, z) = (2, 5, 0)$ with value 14. Can you verify the two constraints are active? ::: ## Example 14.7: Solving the Morra Game 3-finger Morra: each player shows 1-3 fingers and guesses the opponent's number; a correct guess wins the total shown. 9 pure strategies; a **zero-sum game** solved by two linear programs (one per player). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} solve.game <- function(A) { min.A <- min(A); A <- A - min.A; max.A <- max(A); A <- A / max(A) # so that v >= 0 m <- nrow(A); n <- ncol(A); it <- n^3 a <- c(rep(0, m), 1) # maximize v for player 1 A1 <- -cbind(t(A), rep(-1, n)); b1 <- rep(0, n) A3 <- t(as.matrix(c(rep(1, m), 0))); b3 <- 1 sx <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, A3 = A3, b3 = b3, maxi = TRUE, n.iter = it) a <- c(rep(0, n), 1) # minimize v for player 2 A1 <- cbind(A, rep(-1, m)); b1 <- rep(0, m) A3 <- t(as.matrix(c(rep(1, n), 0))); b3 <- 1 sy <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, A3 = A3, b3 = b3, maxi = FALSE, n.iter = it) list("A" = A * max.A + min.A, "x" = sx$soln[1:m], "y" = sy$soln[1:n], "v" = sx$soln[m + 1] * max.A + min.A) } A <- matrix(c(0, -2, -2, 3, 0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, -3, -3, 4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, -4, -4, -3, 0, -3, 0, 4, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0, 3, 0, -4, 0, -4, 0, 5, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 4, 0, -5, 0, -5, -4, -4, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0, 6, 0, 0, 4, -5, -5, 0, 0, 0, 6, 0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 5, -6, -6, 0), 9, 9) sol <- solve.game(A) round(cbind(player1 = sol$x, player2 = sol$y), 7); sol$v ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` player1 player2 x1 0.0000 0.0000 x2 0.0000 0.0000 x3 0.4098 0.4098 x4 0.0000 0.0000 x5 0.3279 0.3279 x6 0.0000 0.0000 x7 0.2623 0.2623 x8 0.0000 0.0000 x9 0.0000 0.0000 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x10 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - The game is symmetric, so its value is 0. The simplex solution puts weight 25/61, 20/61, 16/61 on strategies (1,3), (2,2), (3,1); this is one of the extreme points of the set of optimal strategies discussed in the book. ::: ## Python Supplement: `scipy.optimize` ```{.python} import numpy as np from scipy import optimize, special, stats x = stats.gamma(a=5, scale=1/2).rvs(size=200, random_state=4750) def nll(eta): r, lam = np.exp(eta) return -np.sum(stats.gamma.logpdf(x, a=r, scale=1/lam)) fit = optimize.minimize(nll, x0=[0, 0], method="BFGS") print(np.exp(fit.x)) res = optimize.linprog(c=[-2, -2, -3], A_ub=[[-2, 1, 1], [4, -1, 3]], b_ub=[1, 3]) # Example 14.6 print(res.x, -res.fun) ``` ## Summary ::: instructions - 1-d: `optimize()` (golden section + parabolic interpolation); roots of the score: `uniroot()`. - Multi-d: `optim()`; Nelder-Mead (default), BFGS/L-BFGS-B with gradients, SANN for rough surfaces. - Newton is fast near the optimum; gradient methods are cheap per step; quasi-Newton is the usual compromise. - Reparametrize to remove constraints, use log-scale functions, start from MOM. - Linear programs (`boot::simplex`): optima at vertices; zero-sum games. :::
